title: Dropped affordability argument
resolution: A city ought to abolish minimum parking requirements for new housing.

units.text: Parking minimums raise rents because every tenant pays for mandated construction, even without owning a car.
Frequent transit means many downtown residents can reach work without private vehicles.
Removing minimums can increase cruising when visitors search for scarce curb spaces.
Late-night and weekend transit gaps undermine the claim that residents can reliably avoid cars.
The proposal applies downtown, where all-night bus routes and weekend rail directly answer the service-gap objection.
Delivery drivers also compete for limited curb access during business hours.

title: One rebuttal cross-applied to two claims
resolution: Employers ought to adopt a four-day workweek without reducing pay.

units.text: A shorter week reduces burnout because workers receive an additional recovery day.
It also improves retention because employees value the additional recovery day.
Both benefits assume a real day off, but fixed workloads are compressed into longer shifts and spill into the fifth day, so the promised recovery time disappears for U1 and U2 alike.
Customer support may also become harder to schedule across five weekdays.
Workload caps and a ban on fifth-day messaging preserve the recovery day, directly answering the compression objection.
Rotating teams can maintain customer coverage on every weekday.
